items.title: A notice board needs a scientific explanation
items.student: Fictional school cases: (A) A lunchbox left in sunlight feels warmer than a similar box indoors. (B) A metal gate shows reddish-brown patches after a wet season. (C) A garden team records fewer seedlings after a dry week. For each, list what is directly reported, one question about the natural/material world, evidence you would collect and a possible benefit of investigating. Do not open, taste or handle unknown substances. Record an initial answer: What makes a question scientific? Table headings: case; observation; question; evidence; possible benefit.
items.teacher: Reported observations are warmth, reddish-brown patches and lower seedling count, not established causes. Appropriate questions concern heat transfer, material corrosion and living plants/water, respectively. Investigations need observable/measurable evidence and explanations open to revision. General Science integrates knowledge and inquiry about living things, matter/chemical change and physical processes; these examples connect its areas without rigid boundaries. A value judgement such as which gate colour is prettiest is not settled by measurement alone. Accept other testable questions; do not claim the observations prove a cause.

items.title: Observation or inference?
items.student: Classify each statement as reported observation, inference or question: 1 The paper beside the closed window is wet. 2 Rain must have entered through a gap. 3 A cup on the sill is empty. 4 Someone may have spilled water. 5 Where did the water come from? 6 The window frame has droplets on it. Construct two explanations compatible with at least two observations. Propose one safe additional observation that would help distinguish them; do not accuse a person.
items.teacher: 1,3,6 observations; 2,4 inferences; 5 question. Rain entering and a spill are plausible alternatives; condensation is another candidate if justified. An empty cup is not proof of a spill. Inspecting weather records or asking whether water was placed there can help; each has limitations. Distinguish an observation report from the reliability of its measurement. Inference is a reasoned interpretation of evidence, not certain knowledge of an unseen cause.

items.title: Collect, organise and interpret absorption evidence
items.student: Question: Does paper type affect how far water travels in 60 seconds? Optional teacher-supervised paper-only trial: equal-width strips of two clean paper types, same immersion depth, clean water in shallow stable trays; keep strips vertical and time 60 seconds. Measure rise from the starting water line. Three fresh strips per type. Table: paper type; trial 1; trial 2; trial 3; mean rise (mm). Printed illustrative fallback: A 18,20,22 mm; B 9,10,11 mm. Calculate means, describe the pattern, infer which paper showed greater rise under these conditions, and state a limitation. Never claim these values came from your own experiment if you used the printed data.
items.teacher: Prepare identical-width strips and rulers, protect desks, keep water away from electricity, wipe spills; the teacher sets up trays before class. Printed means A20 mm and B10 mm. Repeat readings help reveal variation; same strip dimensions, water, immersion depth and time improve comparability. Paper A shows greater mean rise in this small trial; the result does not establish every property of the paper or prove a microscopic explanation. Actual results may differ and must be recorded honestly. Printed analysis provides inference/data skills, not evidence of hands-on measuring. Offer large-print tables or verbal description with a scribe.

items.title: Do the seedlings identify a cause?
items.student: Illustrative records, not a real experiment: tray P had 10 seedlings Monday and 6 Friday; tray Q had 10 Monday and 9 Friday. P received 20 mL water daily and Q 40 mL. P was in a sunny room; Q in a cooler shaded room. State two observations and an inference. Is water amount alone established as the cause? Identify a competing explanation and plan a fairer comparison. Use written plans only; no growing practical is required. Plan headings: question; changed factor; factors kept comparable; measured outcome; repeats; limitation.
items.teacher: Losses P4 and Q1; observed counts differ. Less water may contribute, but light/temperature/location also differ, and counts alone do not identify mechanism. A fairer comparison varies water amount with comparable seed type, initial condition, soil, container, light and temperature, measures a defined outcome over a fixed interval and uses several trays per condition. Avoid claiming one extra observation proves causation. Learners may identify initial health or pests as alternatives if they state these were not measured.

items.title: Printed career evidence and chart
items.student: Source summaries, checked 13 November 2026; paraphrases, not quotations. Source A: Kenya Meteorological Department, About Us, https://meteo.go.ke/organization/about/ — its work includes weather/climate observations, analysis, forecasting and early warnings. Source B: Kenya Medical Research Institute, Background, https://www.kemri.go.ke/background/ — its national research role concerns human health. From these summaries identify two related career directions: weather/climate science and human-health research. Construct a chart with columns career direction; science questions; evidence used; possible community benefit; source support; further information needed. Distinguish stated institutional roles from your suggested examples. Choose one direction of interest, explain your reason and write one question to investigate about training. These summaries do not specify qualifications or guarantee employment. Optional teacher-approved digital check during the source-check slot: on a supplied device open one named official page, identify its title/URL, locate a statement about a scientific process or benefit and distinguish that statement from your suggested career activity. Do not enter personal data or follow unrelated links. The printed route remains available; it does not demonstrate digital navigation.
items.teacher: Weather/climate scientist is a reasonable inference from A; suggested evidence includes instrument measurements and weather records. Human-health researcher is a reasonable inference from B; suggested evidence might include appropriately governed study data. The sources support institutional roles, not every proposed job title, duty, qualification or salary. Require learners to label proposed questions/evidence as examples and training as unverified. Display/print these summaries so internet access is optional. Invite a qualified local resource person only if arranged; do not invent a visit. Each learner produces an individual chart before peer discussion. Assess reasons and evidence, not preference for a particular career. Digital route: precheck/open the official pages or cached official copies and use the 4-minute source-check slot only where enough devices and observation opportunities exist. Each participating learner should perform one navigation/retrieval action, identify title/URL and supported statement, and handle the device appropriately. Record learner | observed action/evidence | independent/prompted/not observed. For print-only work explicitly record digital literacy and responsible device use “not observed”; a partner’s navigation is not the learner’s evidence. If access/timing prevents observation, retain print learning and plan a later accessible digital station before claiming that competency. Do not equate author browsing or reading a URL with learner digital competence.

items.title: A science-use message for the community
items.student: Using GS11–GS15, prepare a one-page message answering: How is General Science useful in daily life? Include one life, one environment and one technology example; explain the evidence-to-decision link in each. Add a small career chart and a personal next learning action. Exchange messages: identify one supported claim, one overclaim and a question. Revise in a different colour. You may use the paper absorption case for technology: selecting a material for a specified job still requires testing the relevant property. Avoid giving health treatment or real weather-warning advice.
items.teacher: Possible links: questions about living things guide garden investigations; evidence about water/materials informs environmental decisions; tested properties guide design/material selection. Distinguish established trial evidence from suggested application. One absorption test cannot certify a product for every use. Keep career information within GS15 source limits. Respectful critique concerns a claim, not a person. Individual reflection provides formative evidence of appreciation and interest, not a claim to observe enduring attitude change.

items.title: Independent evidence set
items.student: New fictional case: after equal 60-second tests, three strips of material X show water rise 12,14,16 mm; Y shows 6,8,10 mm. Strip width, water source and immersion depth were the same; X was tested in sunlight and Y in shade. Observers report water lines and times. A poster claims: “X is always the best material; sunlight is irrelevant.” Career source summaries: A, Kenya Meteorological Department About Us (https://meteo.go.ke/organization/about/), describes observations, analysis, forecasts and early warnings. B, KEMRI Background (https://www.kemri.go.ke/background/), identifies a human-health research role. These are printed paraphrases, not qualification advice. Use only this sheet for the independent task.
items.teacher: Keep separate from teaching cards until Lesson 7. Mean rises X14 mm and Y8 mm. Observations support a difference in this test, while unequal sunlight is a confound and “always best” exceeds the property/context tested. Evidence can inform a proposed material choice but requires controlled checking. Career inferences and institutional statements must remain distinguishable. This is the assessment data set; exemplars belong only in the separate key.
